motions.item_title: A Resolution of Eagle Mountain City, Utah, Amending the Consolidated Fee Schedule for Water, Sewer, and Storm Water Rates. Assistant to the City Administrator Evan Berrett presented the item. The proposed changes are being brought to the City Council at this time due to the state of the water fund. Staff estimates that with no changes, the water fund balance will be depleted by Fiscal Year (FY) 2024. The current rates were set in 2010 and the tiers make little to no impact for 96% of residents. U.S. water and wastewater rates increase 4.9% on average each year. As the City expands and ages, the growing cost to maintain infrastructure outpaces the new revenues from additional customers. The cost of water also increases over time, and operational costs increase due to inflation, among other reasons. Mr. Berrett noted that current tiers greatly overestimate actual water use and do not encourage conservation. Eagle Mountain is one of two test cities for the Utah State University LiDar Imagery used to classify landscapes and determine actual water needs for properties compared to usage. The data collected indicated that many Eagle Mountain residents are watering their lawns nearly three times a much as they need to be. Utah Code 73-10-32.5 requires water rate structures with the intent to improve water conservation. Because the City did not implement a 1.5% annual increase to meet rising costs, residents will now see a larger increase. Projected increased operational costs and the costs of obtaining water will require future rate increases every three years at a minimum. Two water rate solutions ultimately received in-depth analysis. The first solution was to modify the rates but maintain the tier structure resulting in an average increase to rates of approximately 25% with 3% annual increases until FY 2032. The second solution is to modify both the rates and the tier structures, resulting in an average increase to rates of approximately 28% with a 3% annual increase until FY 2032. Each solution would maintain the separate residential rates for lots smaller or larger than 0.5 acre. The second solution modifies the tier structures for each customer class to match the actual usage better, increases conservation incentives, and recovers the fund balance faster. Either option results in an immediate increase in usage rate and a base rate increase of $5.50, decreasing in FY 2026 by $2.00. Commercial and institutional uses would also have tier rate adjustments to better reflect usage to be more effective with conservation. Industrial rates will be increased to a set uniform rate which is common for other cities with various industries including data centers, depending upon the amount of conservation pressure desired by the Council. Discussion ensued regarding the following items: • The necessity to raise water rates; • The impact of the water reserve fund on the City’s ability to bond; • The plans to regularly review the rates to ensure they are appropriate and sufficient, • State water conservation requirements; • The amount of conservation incentivization the Council feels is appropriate for residential and nonresidential uses; • The inability of the City to address water issues through slowing residential growth with consideration of the housing shortage; • Offering lower rates for larger lots to encourage large lot development and water usage reduction per acre; and • Ensuring that rates are proportional to prevent users from subsidizing the rates of other types of use. Mayor Pro Tempore Love expressed her support for the rate and tier modification with a 4% increase due to considerations of the water fund reserve. Councilmembers Wright, Gray, and Curtis expressed their preference for the rate modification option maintaining the current tier system as long as it will not negatively impact the City's ability to bond. Councilmember Curtis stated that residents can contact Utah State University for guidance on the proper amount of water needed for their lawns. Mr. Berrett said the library has lawn water kits available for residents to check their watering level needs. Mr. Berrett explained that the sewer rates are still in review and will be presented at a future meeting. The Storm Water fund has struggled for some time. Fund transfers from Solid Waste have been insufficient to keep the fund stable, and transfers will soon no longer be a possibility. To achieve sufficient ongoing revenue to meet fund balance goals, the stormwater rate would need to increase from $5.00 to $8.25 per equivalent residential unit, a 65% increase. Raising the rate as indicated would hold the fund balance steady for five to six fiscal years; around FY 2028 the fund balance would begin to grow and potentially meet the reserve fund balance need. The Solid Waste fund does not currently need to be altered. However, expenses will exceed revenues around FY 2030, and rates will likely need to be changed at that time.
motions.motion: Councilmember Wright moved to table a resolution of Eagle Mountain, City, Utah, amending the Consolidated Fee Schedule for water, sewer, and stormwater rates. Councilmember Curtis seconded the motion. Those voting aye: Donna Burnham, Jared Gray, Colby Curtis, Carolyn Love, and Brett Wright. The motion passed with a unanimous vote.
